# Electromagnetism and induction (`electromagnetism`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electric_battery; helped by magnetic_compass, wire_drawing
- Core idea: A wire carrying current deflects a compass needle held near it: the current is surrounded by a circular magnetic force. Wind insulated wire (wrapped in silk or cotton thread, or varnished) in many turns round a bar of soft iron and it becomes a strong magnet while the current flows and loses its force when the current stops; this is the electromagnet, the basis of telegraph, relay, bell and motor. The reverse also holds: moving a magnet into or out of a coil, or switching the current in a neighbouring coil on or off, drives a current in the coil, but only while something is changing (induction). This is the basis of dynamo and transformer.
- Pitfalls:
  - Bare wire wound on iron: the turns short-circuit and nothing happens; every turn must be insulated from its neighbours and from the core
  - Expecting a steady magnet at rest in a coil to produce current; only change induces
  - Using hard steel for an electromagnet core: it stays magnetised; use soft annealed iron
  - Holding the compass at right angles to the wire instead of laying the wire along the needle, so the effect is missed, as it was for twenty years
- History: europe: 1802 – Romagnosi reports a needle disturbed by a voltaic pile (ignored, and its meaning is disputed); 1820 Ørsted in Copenhagen, then Ampère, forces between currents, and Schweigger's multiplier coil; c. 1824–1825 Sturgeon's electromagnet; 1831 Faraday, induction; americas: 1829–1831 – Joseph Henry at Albany builds strong electromagnets with many turns of silk-insulated wire and finds self-induction; his work on induction is independent of Faraday but published later
- Read:
  - Hans Christian Ørsted, Experimenta circa effectum conflictus electrici in acum magneticam (1820)
  - Michael Faraday, Experimental Researches in Electricity, vol. 1 (1839)
  - Nancy Forbes & Basil Mahon, Faraday, Maxwell, and the Electromagnetic Field (2014)
